content: 1. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 2. HIV virological assays for clinical diagnostic testing, typically performed at or after six weeks of age, should have a sensitivity of at least 95% (ideally greater than 98%) and a specificity of 98% or more under standardized, validated laboratory conditions. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 3. HIV virological testing is strongly recommended for diagnosing HIV infection in infants and children under 18 months of age. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence. 4. For infants and children undergoing virological testing, the following assays are strongly recommended: HIV DNA on whole blood or dried blood spots (DBS), HIV RNA on plasma or DBS, and ultrasensitive p24 antigen on plasma or DBS. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 5. All HIV-exposed infants should undergo HIV virological testing at 4–6 weeks of age or at the earliest opportunity thereafter. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. 6. If an infant has an initial positive virological test result, antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated immediately without delay. At the same time, a second specimen should be collected to confirm the initial positive result. ART initiation should not be delayed while awaiting confirmatory test results, as immediate treatment saves lives. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 7. Test results from virological testing in infants should be returned to the clinic and the child/mother/caregiver as soon as possible, ideally within four weeks of specimen collection. Positive results should be fast-tracked to the mother-baby pair to enable prompt initiation of ART. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 8. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 9. HIV-exposed infants who are well should undergo HIV serological testing at around nine months of age or during their last immunization visit. Infants with reactive serological assays at nine months should have a virological test to confirm HIV infection and determine the need for ART. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 10. Infants with signs or symptoms suggestive of HIV infection should undergo HIV serological testing. If the result is positive (reactive), virological testing should follow. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 11. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 12. Adding nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth to existing early infant diagnosis (EID) testing approaches can be considered to identify HIV infection in HIV-exposed infants. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 13. NAT technologies validated for use at or near the point of care can be used for early infant HIV testing. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 14. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 15. RDTs for HIV serology can be used at nine months to rule out HIV infection in asymptomatic HIV-exposed infants. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 16. RDTs for HIV serology can diagnose HIV infection in children older than 18 months, following the national testing strategy. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 17. In generalized epidemic settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics should be routinely tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 18. In generalized epidemic settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status should be offered HIV testing in outpatient or immunization clinics. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 19. HIV testing services should be routinely offered to all key populations in community, closed, and facility-based settings. Community-based HIV testing services linked to prevention, treatment, and care are recommended in addition to routine facility-based testing. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 20. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 21. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 22. ART should be initiated in all adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 23. ART should be started in all TB patients living with HIV, regardless of CD4 count. TB treatment should be initiated first, followed by ART as soon as possible within the first eight weeks of TB treatment. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 24. Routine viral load monitoring is recommended at six months, 12 months, and annually thereafter for patients stable on ART. Viral load is the preferred approach to diagnose and confirm treatment failure. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 25. Second-line ART for adults and adolescents should consist of two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI). Specific NRTI backbones are recommended based on the failure of first-line regimens. 26. Infants born to mothers with HIV at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with zidovudine (AZT) and nevirapine (NVP) for the first six weeks of life. Breastfed infants at high risk should continue prophylaxis for an additional six weeks. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 27. National health authorities should decide whether to counsel and support HIV-infected mothers to breastfeed with ARV interventions or avoid breastfeeding entirely. In settings promoting breastfeeding, mothers should exclusively breastfeed for the first six months and continue breastfeeding for 12 months while introducing complementary foods. Breastfeeding should stop only when a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence for the first six months and low-quality evidence for 12 months.
